Simultaneously filling process and mechanism of through-hole and blind hole by
copper electroplating
Yuhan Dai , Xiaonan Zhao , Jie Chen , Zhenyu Wang and Ning Xiao
College of Chemical Engineering, Beijing University of Chemical Technology, Beijing, People’s Republic of China
ABSTRACT
In this study, a traditional copper electroplating formula was used to fill microvias, which indicated
that when the concentrations of Janus Green B (JGB) and bis-(sodium sulphopropyl) disulphide
(SPS) were both controlled at 6 mg L<sup>−1</sup>, through-holes and blind holes can be simultaneously and
perfect filled with deposited copper by regulating the convection intensity. As a result, the dimple
at the mouth of through-hole was only 5 μm, and the filling performance of blind hole was 88%.
Galvanostatic measurements (GMs) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) were employed to
study the microvia filling mechanism. It demonstrated that the plating solution in the centre of
the through-hole was nearly stagnant under the weak convection, which resulted in the
accelerator SPS being preferentially adsorbed and further enhanced the copper deposition here. It
led to the formation of butterfly-like deposited copper layer in the through-hole and finally filled
the through-holes and blind holes simultaneously.

1. Introduction
To meet the demands of modern electronic products for mul-
tifunctionality and miniaturisation, high-density interconnect
(HDI) technology has been widely adopted in the advanced
manufacturing of printed circuit boards (PCBs), particularly
in fields such as 5G communications and wearable
devices<sup>1–3</sup>. Currently, the integration of blind holes and
through-holes plays a critical role in HDI for multilayer PCBs;
the filling process of blind holes and through-holes is one
of the key technologies for HDI<sup>4,5</sup>. Typically, there are two
main methods for filling through-holes and blind holes. The
first method involves filling the holes with insulating resin
or conductive paste after the metallisation. However, due to
diferences in the coeficients of thermal expansion (CTE)
between the resin and copper, prolonged usage may com-
promise the reliability of the PCB<sup>6,7</sup>. The second method
involves the complete filling of through-holes and blind
holes with copper electroplating. This approach not only
achieves electrical interconnection but also significantly
shortens the PCB production cycle through a one-step hole-
filling process. Additionally, it markedly enhances the
reliability, conductivity, thermal performance and mechanical
properties of HDI<sup>8–10</sup>. Therefore, the copper electroplating for
through-holes and blind holes has become the mainstream
process to meet the requirements of HDI<sup>11</sup>.
For through-hole plating, the relatively complex pulse
electroplating technique has been commonly employed<sup>12–14</sup>.
Zhang et al.<sup>15</sup> optimised the periodic reverse pulse plating
process using numerical simulation methods, achieving con-
formal filling of through-holes with an aspect ratio of 10:1.
Ning et al.<sup>16</sup> utilised horizontal pulse copper electroplating
technology to successfully achieve conformal thickening of
high-aspect-ratio through-holes and super-filling of blind
holes, ultimately obtaining a smooth copper layer. Compared
to the complex pulse electroplating process, direct current
(DC) copper electroplating ofers advantages such as lower
equipment costs, simpler operational parameters and higher
process stability. Liu et al.<sup>9</sup> developed an electroplating sol-
ution formulation suitable for the simultaneous filling of
through-holes and blind holes, which can be implemented
using only a direct current (DC) power supply. Additionally,
they optimised the process by improving the pattern plating
method, thereby minimising the thickness of the surface
copper. Zhao et al.<sup>17</sup> employed 1-dodecyl-2-methyl-3-benzyli-
midazolium chloride (DMBI) as a leveller, successfully achieving
conformal thickening in through-holes and void-free filling in
blind holes. In situ ATR-SEIRAS spectroscopy and electrochemi-
cal experiments revealed that DMBI inhibits the electroreduc-
tion of copper ions by competing with SPS. Currently, the
simultaneous electroplating process for through-holes and
blind holes primarily focuses on achieving conformal thicken-
ing of through-holes. However, this conformal thickening
approach may lead to reduced signal transmission reliability
and insuficient thermal performance during the long-term
use of HDI<sup>18–20</sup>. To address these issues, it is necessary to
achieve complete filling of through-holes. Therefore, this
study aims to develop an acidic sulphate copper plating
process based on a low-voltage DC power supply to achieve
simultaneous and complete filling of through-holes and
blind holes.
In this study, the commonly used SPS and JGB were
employed as the accelerator and leveller, respectively.
Based on a clear understanding of the efects of convection
intensity and additive concentration on the copper plating
filling performance, a novel method of optimising the filling
efect through gradient regulation of convection intensity
was proposed. This approach successfully achieved simul-
taneous and flawless filling of through-holes and blind
holes, significantly enhancing the metallisation eficiency
of HDI.

3. Results and discussion
3.1. Filling performance efected by convection
intensity
Generally, strong convection can eliminate concentration
gradients in the plating solution, improving the quality of
the deposited copper. Based on this, a microvia filling exper-
iment was conducted under continuous strong convection
and the results are shown in Figure 1.
It can be seen that a super conformal model had taken
place in the blind hole, while the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling
model could not be achieved inside the through-holes,
because, under strong convection, the plating solution
flowed directly through the through-hole, which resulted
in relatively strong convection in the centre of the
through-holes like that on the PCB surface. Consequently,
the distribution of additives inside and outside the
through-hole was similar. According to the CDA model,
the accelerator molecules could not accumulate in the
centre of through-holes, which finally led to conforma
copper deposition in through-holes. At this stage, the
surface was relatively smooth. The copper deposition thick-
ness inside the through-holes and on the PCB surface was
approximately 15 μm, and the dimple at the mouth of the
blind hole was 33 μm.
Given that the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling model could not be
achieved in the through-hole under continuous strong con-
vection, the convection intensity was subsequently reduced
to enhance the adsorption of accelerator molecules inside
the hole. As shown in Figure. 2, copper electroplating for
filling through-hole and blind hole were carried out under
continuous weak convection.
As expected, the ‘butterfly-shaped’ copper layer was
observed in the through-hole and led to good filling perform-
ance. In addition, the blind hole was also well filled by the
deposited copper under continuous weak convection – an
average depth of 17 μm at the mouth of the through-holes
and a reduction to 15 μm at the blind holes. However, the
PCB surface morphology exhibited nodules and vertical stria-
tions, indicating significant degradation, which could be

intensity

through-hole was similar. According to the CDA model,
the accelerator molecules could not accumulate in the
centre of through-holes, which finally led to conforma

surface was relatively smooth. The copper deposition thick-

and a reduction to 15 μm at the blind holes. However, the
PCB surface morphology exhibited nodules and vertical stria-
tions, indicating significant degradation, which could be
attributed to the gradual depletion of surface copper ions
and additives as the electroplating progressed. The resulting
concentration gradients in the plating solution cannot be
efectively eliminated through difusion, leading to a signifi-
cant deterioration in surface morphology, resulting in the for-
mation of vertical striations, nodules and other surface
defects.

Based on the above results, the following microvia filling
experiments were conducted by using a method of regulat-
ing the convection intensity gradient. For through-holes,
once the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling model had taken place
and the ‘bridge’ was formed at the centre of the through-
hole, it could be approximated as two symmetrical blind-
holes. To determine the ‘bridge’ time, microvia filling exper-
iments were first conducted under weak convection.
As shown in Figure 3, a ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling trend
emerged in the through-holes and a ‘bottom-up’ filling
trend was observed in the blind holes. After 40 min of electro-
plating, the thickness of the copper layer on the PCB surface
was 6 μm, while the copper layer thickness inside the through
hole and the blind hole reached 42 and 15 μm, respectively.
When the electroplating time reached 50 min, the surface
copper thickness was 14 μm, the copper layers on both
sides of the through-hole had bridged, and the copper thick-
ness inside the blind hole reached 40 μm. Specifically, the
copper deposition rates at the centre of the through-holes
and the bottom of the blind holes were both higher than
that on the surface. This copper deposition behaviour was
beneficial for achieving void-free filling in both through-
holes and blind holes. As shown in Figure 3(c1), after electro-
plating for 50 min, the deposited copper layer inside the
through-hole successfully converged and formed the
‘bridge’. As a result, the through-hole was divided into two
similar blind holes.
For blind holes, appropriately strong convection was facili-
tated to increase the diference of copper deposition rate
between the PCB surface and the bottom. Therefore, after
the ‘bridge’ was formed inside the through-hole, switching
to strong convection could enhance the filling performance
of both through-holes and blind holes as well as improve
the surface morphology of the deposited copper layer. To
determine the optimal convection intensity switching time,
the microvia filling results obtained at diferent switching
times were investigated, as shown in Figure 4.
After electroplating for 40 min, the ‘butterfly-shaped
filling trend in the through-hole was apparent, but the
‘bridge’ in the through-hole had not yet occurred,
let alone the complete filling of the through-hole. It indi-
cated that switching the forced convection from weak to
strong before the ‘bridge’ formation would hinder the com-
pletion of through-hole filling, even if the ‘butterfly-shaped
filling trend emerged. This result can be attributed to the
unique geometry of through-holes. In the through-hole,
accelerator molecules were dificult to adsorb onto the
inner surface of the through-hole under the strong convec-
tion, which prevented the formation of the ‘bridge’. It indi-
cated that only after ‘bridging’ was complete in the
through-hole and transformed it into two symmetrical
blind holes, could switching to strong convection be facili-
tated to achieve perfect filling and obtain smooth deposited
copper layer. In addition, it could be concluded from Figure
4 that the optimal electroplating process was first electro-
plating for 60 min under weak convection, then switching
to strong convection and continue electroplating for

once the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling model had taken place
and the ‘bridge’ was formed at the centre of the through-
hole, it could be approximated as two symmetrical blind-
holes. To determine the ‘bridge’ time, microvia filling exper-
iments were first conducted under weak convection.
As shown in Figure 3, a ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling trend
emerged in the through-holes and a ‘bottom-up’ filling
trend was observed in the blind holes. After 40 min of electro-
plating, the thickness of the copper layer on the PCB surface
was 6 μm, while the copper layer thickness inside the through
hole and the blind hole reached 42 and 15 μm, respectively.
When the electroplating time reached 50 min, the surface
copper thickness was 14 μm, the copper layers on both
sides of the through-hole had bridged, and the copper thick-
ness inside the blind hole reached 40 μm. Specifically, the
copper deposition rates at the centre of the through-holes
and the bottom of the blind holes were both higher than
that on the surface. This copper deposition behaviour was
beneficial for achieving void-free filling in both through-
holes and blind holes. As shown in Figure 3(c1), after electro-
plating for 50 min, the deposited copper layer inside the
through-hole successfully converged and formed the
‘bridge’. As a result, the through-hole was divided into two
similar blind holes.
For blind holes, appropriately strong convection was facili-
tated to increase the diference of copper deposition rate
between the PCB surface and the bottom. Therefore, after
the ‘bridge’ was formed inside the through-hole, switching
to strong convection could enhance the filling performance
of both through-holes and blind holes as well as improve
the surface morphology of the deposited copper layer. To
determine the optimal convection intensity switching time,
the microvia filling results obtained at diferent switching
times were investigated, as shown in Figure 4.
After electroplating for 40 min, the ‘butterfly-shaped
filling trend in the through-hole was apparent, but the
‘bridge’ in the through-hole had not yet occurred,
let alone the complete filling of the through-hole. It indi-
cated that switching the forced convection from weak to
strong before the ‘bridge’ formation would hinder the com-
pletion of through-hole filling, even if the ‘butterfly-shaped
filling trend emerged. This result can be attributed to the
unique geometry of through-holes. In the through-hole,
accelerator molecules were dificult to adsorb onto the
inner surface of the through-hole under the strong convec-
tion, which prevented the formation of the ‘bridge’. It indi-
cated that only after ‘bridging’ was complete in the
through-hole and transformed it into two symmetrical
blind holes, could switching to strong convection be facili-
tated to achieve perfect filling and obtain smooth deposited
copper layer. In addition, it could be concluded from Figure
4 that the optimal electroplating process was first electro-
plating for 60 min under weak convection, then switching
to strong convection and continue electroplating for

3.3. Microvia filling mechanism
The GMs were carried out in the optimal electroplating sol-
ution under diferent rotation speeds and the results are
shown in Figure 7. It could be noted that the copper depo-
sition potential increased gradually with the increase of
rotation speed, which could lead to decrease of the copper
deposition rate. Under both weak and strong convection,
the copper deposition rate at the centre of the through-
hole and the bottom of the blind hole is faster than that on
the PCB surface. This indicates that SPS showed stronger
adsorption strength than that of JGB in these regions. Actu-
ally, according to CDA theory, SPS preferentially adsorbed
onto the surface where the convection was relatively
weaker, such as in the centre of the through-hole and on
the bottom of the blind hole, thereby accelerating the
copper deposition rate in these regions. It finally resulted in
the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling in through-holes and the
‘bottom-up’ filling in blind holes.
According to the electrochemical experimental results, the
copper deposition process became increasingly dificult with
the enhancement of convective intensity (electrode rotation
speed).

spans.content: Therefore, to clarify the velocity diferences between the
inside and outside of the through-hole under weak convec-
tive during the initial stage of electroplating, and to reveal
the formation mechanism of the ‘butterfly’ filling behaviour
within the through-hole, computational fluid dynamics
(CFD) were conducted on the through-hole structure. The
simulation results are shown in Figure 8.
Figure 8a is a schematic diagram of the fluid simulation
model. The calculation result is shown in Figure 8b. The red
arrows indicate velocity vectors with higher speeds, while
the blue arrows represent vectors with lower speeds.
Under the influence of the electric field, the solution
flowed from the bulk towards the PCB surface, with the vel-
ocity concentrated outside the PCB surface. When the sol-
ution flowed into the through-hole, the velocity
significantly increased at the hole entrance due to the diam-
eter restriction and flow convergence. After entering the
through-hole, the flow converged at the centre of the
hole. Due to the spatial constraints inside the through-
hole, the velocity vectors within the hole were nearly sym-
metrical, and their resultant vector approached zero. This
indicates that the plating solution at the centre of the
through-hole was almost stationary. This velocity distri
bution pattern resulted in the flow rate outside the
through-hole being significantly higher than that inside
the through-hole. Combined with the electrochemical
testing results, the copper deposition potential under
stationary conditions is lower than that under weak convec-
tion. As a result, copper preferentially deposited at the
centre of the through-hole, which led to the ‘butterfly-
shaped’ filling in the through-hole.

To further reveal the primary and secondary distribution of
additives inside and outside the through-hole before and
after switching the convection intensity, a model of the
through-hole filling development process has been proposed
based on electrochemical testing and fluid simulation results,
as shown in Figure 9.
Figure 9a,b represent the distribution of additives during
the initial stage of through-hole filling and the copper depo-
sition development stage inside the through-hole, respectively.
In the initial stage of electroplating; due to the large molecular
weight of the suppressor and the very weak convection inside
the through-hole, most of the suppressor molecules adsorbed
onto the surface outside the through-hole, while JGB molecules
with positive charge accumulated at the mouth of the through
hole, suppressing copper deposition in this region. Inside the
through-hole, the leveller and accelerator molecules were uni-
formly distributed, and the concentration of the suppressor
was relatively low, which resulted in the copper deposition
rate inside the through-hole being higher than that on the
surface. As the electroplating progressed, the adsorption of
the accelerator molecules became dominant at the centre of
the through-hole because the convection intensity here was
relatively weak. Thus, the copper deposition rate at the hole
centre was significantly increased, which ultimately resulted
in the ‘butterfly-shaped’ filling.

Figure 9c illustrates the copper deposition process under
continuous weak convection. Because of the weak convection,
chloride ions and additive molecules could only adsorb onto
the PCB surface and inside the hole through difusion. As elec
troplating progressed, chloride ions on the copper surface
were consumed. Because difusion alone could not supply
chloride ions to the copper surface in time, the leveller and
suppressor gradually desorbed from the copper surface. This
reduced the suppression and levelling abilities for copper
deposition on the PCB surface, ultimately resulting in the
uneven surface of the deposited copper layer.
Figure 9d illustrated the copper deposition process after
achieving a ‘bridge’ inside the through-hole and switching
to strong convection. At this stage, the ‘bridge’ had been
achieved inside the through-hole and changed it into two
symmetrical blind holes. Upon switching to strong convec-
tion, the concentration diferences of the components in
the plating solution were eliminated, and chloride ions as
well as additives on the copper surface were replenished
and re-adsorbed. The accelerator preferentially adsorbed at
the bottom of the blind holes, where the convection was
weak. Meanwhile, the leveller and suppressor preferentially
adsorbed on the surface and at the hole openings, where
the convection was strong. This ultimately resulted in overfi-
lling of the two symmetrical blind holes.
The distribution of additives during the blind hole filling
process was similar to that of through-holes. The convection
intensity being switched from weak to strong could efec-
tively eliminate the concentration diferences in the plating
solution. It promoted the additive molecules to re-adsorb uni-
formly onto the copper surface, finally producing a deposited
copper layer which was smooth and bright.
4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that simultaneous filling of through-
holes and blind holes could not be achieved through continu-
ous strong convection alone. While continuous weak convec-
tion enabled filling, it resulted in uneven copper deposition
surfaces. These challenges were efectively resolved by imple-
menting time-dependent convection control. Using the

4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that simultaneous filling of through-
holes and blind holes could not be achieved through continu-
ous strong convection alone. While continuous weak convec-
tion enabled filling, it resulted in uneven copper deposition
surfaces. These challenges were efectively resolved by imple-
menting time-dependent convection control. Using the
plating solution containing 6 mg L<sup>−1</sup> bis(3-sulphopropyl)
disulphide (SPS) and 6 mg
{ \mathsf { L } } ^ { - 1 }
Janus Green B (JGB), the opti-
mised process involved initial electroplating under weak con-
vection for 60 min to establish a characteristic ‘butterfly-
shaped’ filling pattern and central ‘bridge’ formation within
through-holes. Subsequent switching to strong convection
for 30 min yielded complete void-free filling with superior
surface morphology. Specifically, the depth of the dimple at
the mouth of the through-hole was maintained at 5 μm,
while the blind hole filling eficiency reached 88%.
Electrochemical analysis coupled with CFD simulations
enabled the development of a novel TH filling mechanism
model. The model elucidated two critical phenomena: (1) a
substantial convection gradient existed between the external
and internal through-hole regions and (2) weak convection
conditions promoted lower copper deposition potentials.
These factors synergistically facilitated preferential copper
deposition at the through-hole centre, initiating the charac
teristic butterfly-shaped filling pattern. Following bridge for
mation, the through-hole efectively transformed into two
symmetrical blind holes, allowing subsequent strong convec-
tion to enhance both filling uniformity and surface quality.

Janus Green B (JGB), the opti-
mised process involved initial electroplating under weak con-
vection for 60 min to establish a characteristic ‘butterfly-
shaped’ filling pattern and central ‘bridge’ formation within
through-holes. Subsequent switching to strong convection
for 30 min yielded complete void-free filling with superior
surface morphology. Specifically, the depth of the dimple at
the mouth of the through-hole was maintained at 5 μm,
while the blind hole filling eficiency reached 88%.
Electrochemical analysis coupled with CFD simulations
enabled the development of a novel TH filling mechanism
model. The model elucidated two critical phenomena: (1) a
substantial convection gradient existed between the external
and internal through-hole regions and (2) weak convection
conditions promoted lower copper deposition potentials.
These factors synergistically facilitated preferential copper
deposition at the through-hole centre, initiating the charac
teristic butterfly-shaped filling pattern. Following bridge for
mation, the through-hole efectively transformed into two
symmetrical blind holes, allowing subsequent strong convec-
tion to enhance both filling uniformity and surface quality.
